blocks.text: 1. Stochastic Gradient Descent

blocks.alt: One example produces one gradient estimate, updated immediately

blocks.text: Batch Gradient Descent's genuine speed and memory weaknesses, already covered fully in its own dedicated topic, needed a direct, practical response. Stochastic Gradient Descent was developed specifically to address both of these directly.

It does this by using one single example per weight update, instead of the entire dataset, a dramatically different, far more extreme tradeoff than Batch Gradient Descent's own full-dataset approach already covered in that earlier topic.
2. The Mechanism

blocks.alt: A single example computes a gradient, updating the weights

blocks.text: Stochastic Gradient Descent picks one single training example, computes the gradient using just that one example, and updates every single weight immediately, using that one example's own gradient alone.

It then repeats this exact process with the next example, immediately, meaning weight updates happen far more frequently than under Batch Gradient Descent's own one-update-per-full-pass approach already covered in its own topic.

blocks.text: 3. A Genuine Speed Advantage

blocks.alt: SGD produces many updates per epoch

blocks.text: This connects back to Batch Gradient Descent's own genuine speed weakness, already covered in its own topic. Batch Gradient Descent produces just one weight update per full dataset pass, meaning very few updates happen per unit of actual time on a genuinely large dataset.

Stochastic Gradient Descent instead produces one weight update per single example, dramatically more updates per unit of actual time, directly solving the exact speed problem already covered as Batch Gradient Descent's own genuine weakness.
4. A Genuine, Direct Tradeoff

A genuine, direct tradeoff comes with that speed. A single example is a genuinely noisy, unrepresentative estimate of the true gradient computed across the entire dataset, since any one example may not actually reflect the dataset's own broader, overall pattern well.
Each individual update can point in a somewhat, or even considerably, wrong direction as a result, a genuine cost directly traded against the speed advantage already covered in the previous section.
5. A Noisy Convergence Path

blocks.alt: SGD's path is noisy and zigzagging

blocks.text: This connects back to Batch Gradient Descent's own smooth, predictable loss curve, already covered in its own dedicated topic. Stochastic Gradient Descent's loss curve is genuinely noisy instead, a direct, visible consequence of the per-example noise already covered in the previous section.

The loss bounces around considerably during training, rather than decreasing in one smooth, clean line, a genuinely different, more erratic-looking training trajectory than Batch Gradient Descent's own considerably cleaner path.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: This noisy loss curve is genuinely expected, normal behavior for Stochastic Gradient Descent, not necessarily a sign something has gone wrong. The overall downward trend across many updates still matters more than any single update's own individual noise.

blocks.text: 6. A Genuinely Surprising Benefit: Escaping Local Minima

blocks.alt: A noisy gradient can escape local minima

blocks.text: This connects back to the local minima challenge, already covered in the Gradient Descent topic. A genuinely surprising, real benefit of this exact noise is that the noisy, bouncing updates can actually help escape a shallow local minimum.

A batch-averaged, considerably smoother gradient might otherwise settle into and genuinely get stuck at that same shallow local minimum, meaning Stochastic Gradient Descent's own apparent weakness, noise, doubles as a genuine, real practical advantage in this specific, important situation.
7. A Genuine Memory Advantage

blocks.alt: SGD keeps only one example in memory at a time

blocks.text: This connects back to Batch Gradient Descent's own genuine memory constraint, already covered in its own dedicated topic. Stochastic Gradient Descent only ever needs one single example in memory at any given time, never the entire dataset all at once.

This makes it genuinely practical for datasets of essentially any size, far larger than what could ever fit in memory all at once, directly solving the exact memory limitation already covered as Batch Gradient Descent's own genuine weakness.
8. Motivating Mini-Batch Gradient Descent

This connects forward to Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, covered earlier in this module. It was developed specifically to balance Stochastic Gradient Descent's own genuine speed and noise, both already covered throughout this topic, against Batch Gradient Descent's own genuine accuracy and slowness.

Understanding both Batch and Stochastic Gradient Descent's genuine, opposite tradeoffs clearly sets up direct, considerable groundwork for understanding exactly why Mini-Batch Gradient Descent's own middle-ground approach became the field's genuine, practical default.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Plain SGD Is Still Worth Using

blocks.alt: A huge dataset with limited memory means plain SGD is still worth using

blocks.text: Genuinely massive datasets, where even mini-batches remain impractically slow, are a genuine case where plain Stochastic Gradient Descent's extreme, one-example-at-a-time update frequency, already covered throughout this topic, can genuinely still help.

Most typical, modern Deep Learning training instead finds Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, covered elsewhere in this module, the far more common, practical default, balancing Stochastic's own genuine strengths against its genuine weaknesses considerably better for most real, everyday training scenarios.
10. Worked Example
The example below implements Stochastic Gradient Descent from scratch, directly comparing its update frequency and noise against the Batch Gradient Descent example already covered in its own topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 1))
y = 3 * X.ravel() + 2 + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=200)

weight, bias = 0.0, 0.0
learning_rate = 0.01
epochs = 3

losses = []
for epoch in range(epochs):
    indices = rng.permutation(len(X))
    for i in indices:
        x_i, y_i = X[i, 0], y[i]

        prediction = weight * x_i + bias
        error = prediction - y_i

        # Gradient computed using just ONE example, exactly the stochastic approach covered in this topic
        gradient_weight = error * x_i
        gradient_bias = error

        weight -= learning_rate * gradient_weight
        bias -= learning_rate * gradient_bias
        losses.append(error ** 2)

print(f"Final: weight={weight:.4f}, bias={bias:.4f} (true values: weight=3.0, bias=2.0)")
print(f"Total weight updates across {epochs} epochs: {len(losses)}")
print(f"Loss std deviation across the last 50 updates: {np.std(losses[-50:]):.4f} (genuinely noisy, as expected)")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Notice this example performs one weight update per individual example, resulting in 600 total updates across just 3 epochs on 200 examples, dramatically more than Batch Gradient Descent's single update per epoch, exactly the speed advantage covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Stochastic Gradient Descent uses one single example per weight update, addressing Batch's speed and memory weaknesses.
It picks one example, computes its gradient, updates weights immediately, then repeats with the next example.
It produces dramatically more updates per unit of time than Batch Gradient Descent, a genuine speed advantage.
A single example is a genuinely noisy, unrepresentative gradient estimate, a real, direct tradeoff for that speed.
Its loss curve bounces around considerably, a direct, visible consequence of this per-example noise.
This same noise can genuinely help escape a shallow local minimum a smoother gradient might otherwise get stuck in.
It only needs one example in memory at a time, genuinely practical for datasets of essentially any size.
Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, covered elsewhere in this module, was developed to balance its tradeoffs against Batch's.
It still helps on genuinely massive datasets, though Mini-Batch Gradient Descent is the far more common modern default.
